item.title: OffSec Launches Free PHP2Shell Lab Following Critical Vulnerability Discovery
item.description:
New hands-on lab lets security practitioners explore PHP2Shell exploitation firsthand as AI-assisted research reshapes vulnerability discovery.

OffSec today announced the release of a free, interactive hands-on lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play) to help security practitioners examine and defend against the critical “PHP2Shell” vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) firsthand. Developed in response to AI-accelerated vulnerability discovery and active exploits targeting core PHP engines in the wild, the lab provides penetration testers and enterprise defenders with a safe, controlled environment to study the decade-old memory corruption flaws and implement timely server mitigations.

The two critical flaws sat inside PHP, the language behind roughly 70% of websites whose server-side language is known, for more than a decade. Then researchers at Wiz, a Google-owned cloud security company, pointed AI at the code. 

They found the first flaw Aug. 19. The next day they used it to take over a Drupal site without a password. The day after that, it worked on WordPress.

PHP disclosed the flaws Oct. 21 as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. An attacker with no login can send a series of crafted web requests to crash a server or take it over. PHP’s severity scores rate both vulnerabilities as complex to exploit, even though working attacks already existed. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) recommends patching immediately. 

Attackers are moving fast. Amazon calls PHP2Shell broadly exploited in the wild. By Oct.24, researchers had confirmed attackers running commands on vulnerable honeypot servers. CISA added both flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on Oct. 26. 

“PHP is one of those technologies attackers love to see,” said Keegan Bowen, principal DevOps lead at OffSec. “It has been a great attack vector over the years with many exploits and potential abuses. PHP wasn’t designed with security from the start.”

OffSec, which has taught hands-on offensive security since 2006, has released a free PHP2Shell lab in Proving Grounds Play (PG Play). The lab gives penetration testers and other security professionals a controlled environment to explore CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 firsthand. OffSec’s blog breaks down both flaws, and its proof-of-concept exploit is available on Exploit-DB. 

AI and the Evolving Pace of Exploitation

PHP scored both flaws 9.2 out of 10, a critical rating. To build a working attack, Wiz researchers had to chain several bugs together and tune the attack to each server’s memory. When they let AI do the grind, one researcher finished in a week what once took a top team month. Attackers can use the same AI models, so flaws once ranked too complex to matter are now fair game. 

“At this point, attackers are heavily leaning on AI to find and exploit vulnerabilities; the rate of CVEs is roughly double what was reported last year,” said Matt Freitas-Stavola, staff software engineer at OffSec. “LLMs don’t get tired and can easily run in the background for as long as attackers have money or compute to spare. Even now, just a hint of where an issue could arise is enough for an LLM to get a workable POC out relatively quickly.”

The Effects of These Flaws

Both flaws start with the same weak spot: what PHP does when a request runs out of memory or hits another fatal error.

“PHP is built from C and memory management becomes increasingly challenging as the code grows,” Bowen said. “Some out-of-memory states were not handled well. In some cases, attackers can access interrupted state data before it is cleaned up. That becomes an opportunity for abuse.”

That leftover state can carry into the next request on the same worker. An attacker who shapes it can run code with the web server’s privileges.

The same bugs can also leak data. Wiz showed attackers could potentially read memory from the PHP process. That memory could hold passwords, session tokens, API keys, and certificates from other requests or the server itself. 

The story is still developing. On Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate flaw, CVE-2026-115560, that can affect fully patched servers with an unusual session setup. PHP has no fix for it yet. Researchers have also built PHP2Shell exploits that get past ASLR, a common memory defense, and more issues could surface as the flaws are studied. As research continues, new vulnerabilities, exploitation techniques, and mitigations may emerge beyond those covered here.

OffSec’s Current Recommendations

These steps reflect what is known at the time of publication. Check CISA and the PHP project for the latest recommendations.

  • Patch PHP Now. Update to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35 to address CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Check vendor advisories rather than relying on version numbers alone.
  • Update the Underlying PHP Engine. Updating WordPress, Drupal, or another application does not resolve vulnerabilities in PHP itself. Rebuild affected container images, and restart PHP processes so the updated code takes effect.
  • Apply Temporary Protections While Patching. Disable PHP session upload progress (session.upload_progress.enabled=0), which also mitigates CVE-2026-115560. On PHP 8.5, disable fatal error backtraces and restart affected workers after configuration changes. These measures reduce exposure; they do not replace patching.
  • Investigate Potential Compromise. Review web server and PHP logs for suspicious multipart requests, memory-limit errors, repeated HTTP 500 responses, malformed session cookies, and unexpected PHP worker restarts. Investigations should consider activity dating back to at least October 17, when exploitation attempts were first reported. Rotate potentially affected credentials, API keys, and tokens as appropriate.

Understand the Exploit. Strengthen the Defense.

When the next disclosure lands, someone on the team needs to judge exposure. Reading about an exploit builds awareness. Working on one hands-on builds the skill to respond. 

OffSec’s PHP2Shell lab helps practitioners turn technical knowledge into hands-on experience they can apply to future vulnerabilities. For a deeper look at the vulnerabilities, explore OffSec’s technical analysis. Organizations looking to build these capabilities across their security teams can explore OffSec’s workforce development programs.

OffSec is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

item.title: The infrastructure playbook for operational sovereignty: Why neoclouds need to offer sovereign AI
item.description:
For leadership teams at neoclouds, the explosive demand for AI represents a historic market opportunity. Enterprises are now embedding large language models and autonomous agents directly into their core business automation workflows to manage proprietary patent portfolios, optimize supply chains, and orchestrate customer data.

However, as organizations embed cognitive systems into their operations, a critical structural challenge has emerged: the need for operational sovereignty.

Some multi-tenant cloud ecosystems force enterprises to surrender control over their data pathways and model execution perimeters. For highly regulated industries, public sector entities, and privacy-conscious enterprises, this is an unacceptable risk. By designing and deploying dedicated sovereign AI instances, neoclouds can capture this premium market segment. Providing trust infrastructure, preventing multi-tenant performance degradation and data leakage is no longer just a service differentiator—it could be the ultimate competitive differentiator.

Capturing the premium tier of the sovereign market

When enterprises deploy advanced AI workloads within standard, multi-tenant public cloud frameworks, they expose their core business intelligence to unpredictable out-of-band variables. Hyperscale public environments operate on highly abstracted layers where hardware configurations, resource allocation rules, and network routing pathways can change without notice. An AI workload optimized for specific hardware may experience latency spikes if the background infrastructure shifts to accommodate an unrelated tenant.

For neoclouds, the strategic opportunity lies in solving the auditor’s dilemma for these premium clients. Financial institutions, healthcare providers, and national defense agencies cannot afford to run their high-stakes inference loops on shared public grids where model parameters and operational histories are obscured. If a third-party model vendor changes its API parameters or updates its foundational weights, a client’s downstream autonomous agents can fail instantly.

By building localized, geographic-specific sovereign AI instances, neoclouds can offer asset determinism and data isolation. These dedicated instances can act as a secure vault so the physical location of the data, the location of the hardware running the models, and the personnel maintaining the infrastructure comply with local data residency laws, such as the European Union’s NIS2 Directive or regional sovereign mandates.

Co-engineering the sovereign neocloud engine

To deliver a sovereign environment that rivals the agility of hyperscalers without sacrificing private cloud control, neoclouds require an infrastructure strategy that tightly integrates specialized computing platforms with intelligent cloud management tools. Trying to assemble fragmented hardware clusters manually cannot provide the enterprise-grade stability or compliance tracing required by corporate boards.

This co-engineered computing fabric combines secure-by-design integrated systems with the full-stack power of NVIDIA accelerated computing and networking architectures. Neoclouds can manage this accelerated hardware layer using an intelligent, centralized orchestration plane powered by HPE Morpheus Software. HPE Morpheus acts as the single point of control for the sovereign AI factory, providing cloud-native provisioning, automated resource management, and secure multi-tenant isolation. Through this unified software layer, a neocloud can deliver a public-cloud user experience—allowing enterprise clients to dynamically spin up secure containers, fine-tune open-weight models, and scale workloads via a single interface—while maintaining the physical security, predictable pricing, and ownership of a private enterprise framework.

Insulating the data plane and enforcing execution boundaries

Operating a successful sovereign AI cloud requires continuous, verifiable proof that an enterprise’s data movement is restricted. In an autonomous multi-agent ecosystem, agents continuously pull information from internal relational databases, vector repositories, and real-time streams. If this data crosses unverified network zones or is mixed into a shared cloud plane, the risk of corporate intellectual property leaking into public foundational models escalates.

By anchoring sovereign AI instances within an HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA, neoclouds can deploy advanced data governance tools like the NVIDIA AI Enterprise software suite directly alongside HPE Morpheus orchestration. This joint architecture automates the forensic tracking required for regulatory compliance. Every time a model executes a transaction or triggers an inference pipeline, the infrastructure captures an unalterable, timestamped log of the exact data retrieved, the model weights activated, and the safety guardrails applied. This granular tracing transforms compliance from an expensive administrative burden into a routine, automated validation exercise, giving enterprise CIOs assurance to deploy AI across their most sensitive, localized operations.

item.title: The euro-sovereignty playbook: How telcos are transforming into trusted AI factories
item.description:
Geopolitical reality is transforming digital architecture from a relatively minor procurement detail into a core pillar of corporate risk management. With regulations such as the European Union’s NIS2 Directive and the EU AI Act imposing data residency and algorithmic transparency mandates, global CIOs can no longer outsource their core intelligence infrastructure to generic public clouds. For organizations operating across strict regulatory jurisdictions, data isolation and local operational continuity are no longer secondary objectives—they are essential commercial requirements.

This regulatory landscape has triggered a significant structural shift: regional telecommunications providers are rapidly evolving into sovereign AI factories. By capitalizing on their highly secure, localized networks and existing data center footprints, telcos are providing localized cloud environments engineered explicitly to keep operational data within strictly defined borders. This trend allows enterprises in highly regulated sectors—such as banking, healthcare, and public services—to leverage advanced genAI models without fear of cross-border data leakage or foreign legal interventions.

The mandate for digital self-reliance

The concept of sovereign AI centers on the idea that a nation or a region’s data, intelligence, and underlying digital infrastructure must remain under its own geographic and legal control. When an enterprise trains an AI model on proprietary intellectual property, customer interactions, or national infrastructure data within a public cloud framework, that data often crosses regional borders. This fragmentation subjects the organization to conflicting legal jurisdictions, potential surveillance risks, and the unpredictability of foreign supply chains.

For European enterprise leaders, the stakes are high. Under the NIS2 framework, corporate executives face direct personal liability for cybersecurity and data governance failures within critical entities. Consequently, relying on non-sovereign digital infrastructure introduces compliance liabilities.

To achieve data self-reliance, organizations must migrate their high-stakes genAI workloads to infrastructure that can isolate the data. The physical location of the data, the location of the hardware running the models, and the personnel maintaining the data center are subject to compliance with local statutes. Regional telecommunications companies, long trusted as the guardians of secure national network traffic, are uniquely positioned to fill this void by offering sovereign AI infrastructure as a localized cloud service.

Building the sovereign computing fabric

Evolving from a traditional connectivity provider into a regional AI utility powerhouse requires a new approach to data center design. Processing large-scale AI models requires hardware acceleration, ultra-low latency networking, and industrial-grade software orchestration. To deliver these capabilities without compromising on sovereignty mandates, telcos are turning to optimized, turnkey solutions built by trusted global technology alliances.

These hardware configurations provide the extreme performance required for distributed AI training and high-throughput model inference.

Orchestrating compliance at the regional scale

Operating a sovereign AI factory requires continuous, end-to-end monitoring of both physical and logical data boundaries. It is not enough to simply declare that a server rests within a specific city; enterprise tenants require verifiable proof that data movement is tightly restricted.

To address this demand, telcos leverage specialized orchestration like HPE Morpheus Software alongside NVIDIA’s secure containerization and microservices frameworks. This joint architecture enables strict adherence to localized compliance frameworks by automating audit trails. Every time a model is fine-tuned or an inference pipeline is executed, the infrastructure logs verified records detailing the specific nodes utilized and the localized security protocols applied. This meticulous tracking transforms compliance from a costly administrative burden into a competitive advantage, giving corporate boards the assurance required to deploy AI across sensitive localized operations.

The strategic imperative for global enterprises

Ultimately, the emergence of telco-driven sovereign AI factories provides global organizations with a clear path forward in an increasingly fragmented geopolitical landscape. Rather than pulling back from AI transformation due to regulatory fears, forward-thinking organizations can use these regional clouds to accelerate their digital roadmap safely. By choosing a sovereign infrastructure strategy, your organization’s digital intelligence can remain an exclusive corporate asset, shielded from external geopolitical shocks and aligned with local data governance standards.

item.title: Securing the foundations of intelligence: Physical security and power sovereignty in AI factories
item.description:
As enterprise AI models expand, the competitive advantage belongs to leaders who look beyond software to secure physical infrastructure. Digital autonomy is fundamentally dependent on physical realities: resource availability, power independence, and robust data center supply chains. For the C-suite, long-term operational resilience means designing an infrastructure strategy capable of surviving geopolitical friction, resource scarcity, and unexpected regional power grid shocks.

Today’s AI Factories require unprecedented energy resources to process massive datasets and train specialized models. Consequently, relying solely on centralized public utility infrastructure creates a single point of failure that can compromise an organization’s entire roadmap. Forward-looking IT leaders are treating data center power and location as structural design constraints, investing in regional, modular architectures that shield mission-critical computing environments from external instability.

The physical dependencies of digital sovereignty

When enterprise leaders discuss AI sovereignty, the conversation often gravitates toward data encryption, software firewalls, and data residency laws. However, a model cannot run without compute, and compute cannot exist without a constant, unyielding supply of electricity and physical space. If an external entity or an adversarial state can disrupt the physical facility housing your systems, your software guardrails become irrelevant.

This reality has forced a paradigm shift in how C-level executives evaluate risk. An AI strategy that relies entirely on a handful of mega-scale public data center hubs exposes the organization to systemic vulnerabilities. A regional power outage, a supply chain embargo on critical cooling components, or a localized natural disaster can completely halt an organization’s ability to run inference or execute autonomous workflows.

To help mitigate these physical vulnerabilities, organizations must transition to an infrastructure model that prioritizes physical and power sovereignty. This means establishing private or hybrid AI Factories within highly secure, hardened facilities where the organization retains control over power redundancy, physical access, and equipment maintenance. By decoupling critical compute assets from the shared public grid and multi-tenant public infrastructure, organizations can insulate their core operations from unpredictable macro-level disruptions.

Rethinking density, power, and thermal management

Building a physically sovereign AI factory requires a re-evaluation of data center engineering. Next-generation AI workloads require higher thermal loads, requiring cooling capabilities beyond what standard enterprise server racks can handle. If a data center’s cooling infrastructure fails or is throttled due to environmental regulations or water scarcity, the underlying accelerators will automatically slow or shut down to prevent catastrophic hardware failure.

To address these physical constraints, enterprise technology leaders are leveraging co-engineered systems designed for density, energy efficiency, and operational resilience. Within the HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA, hardware density is optimized to deliver the highest possible compute output per square foot and per watt. By combining HPE liquid-cooling infrastructure with dense, accelerated architectures like the NVIDIA Blackwell platform, organizations can dramatically shrink their physical data center footprint while multiplying their processing capacity.

Liquid cooling is no longer an optional luxury for high-performance computing; it is a foundational security and efficiency requirement. Traditional air-cooled data centers require notable amounts of electricity just to run fan walls and chillers, exposing the organization to fluctuating energy prices and potential power utility caps. By shifting to direct-to-chip liquid cooling systems—engineered through the joint integration of HPE mechanical cooling manifolds and NVIDIA’s high-density accelerated computing architectures—enterprises can slash data center power consumption by up to 40%. This increase in efficiency allows organizations to run their AI factories on localized, modular power generation systems, such as dedicated on-site microgrids or renewable energy installations, achieving more energy independence.

Securing the physical supply chain and operational longevity

Sovereignty also requires long-term visibility into the hardware supply chain. If an organization relies on public cloud providers whose hardware configurations change arbitrarily, it exposes itself to infrastructure lock-in and unexpected operational overhead. A software pipeline optimized for one specific architecture may suffer performance degradation if the cloud vendor silently migrates the workload to a different hardware tier behind the scenes.

By deploying dedicated private infrastructure via the HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA, enterprises regain total control over their physical technology roadmap. C-level executives can rest assured that their critical intellectual property and model states reside on hardware assets that they own or exclusively control. Furthermore, because these systems are built on enterprise-grade lifecycles with guaranteed parts availability and global support ecosystems, the risk of sudden operational disruption due to component obsolescence or foreign supply chain blockades can be reduced.

The C-level physical and power sovereignty readiness checklist

Before scaling your physical AI infrastructure or committing to a long-term data center blueprint, verify that your facilities meet the following operational criteria:

  • Localized energy redundancy: Does your data center strategy include provisions for on-site microgrids, dedicated renewable energy sources, or localized battery storage to shield your AI factory from public utility grid failures?
  • Direct-to-chip liquid cooling: Have you deployed advanced thermal management, such as HPE liquid-cooling infrastructure, to support next-generation compute architectures like the NVIDIA Blackwell platform efficiently?
  • Physical asset determinism: Are your mission-critical model training and inference pipelines running on dedicated, immutable hardware assets, such as the HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA, to prevent unpredictable public cloud migration risks?
  • Hardened perimeter controls: Are the physical facilities housing your computing clusters equipped with multi-factor biometric access controls, isolated security zones, and continuous surveillance to prevent unauthorized physical tampering?
  • Supply chain predictability: Does your infrastructure vendor provide a transparent, long-term hardware support roadmap for consistent component availability and operational continuity over a multi-year horizon? 

Building an ironclad physical foundation

Ultimately, digital intelligence is only as secure as the concrete, steel, and copper that support it. As your organization embeds genAI deeper into its core revenue-generating operations, the physical stability of your compute infrastructure becomes synonymous with business continuity. Investing in private, energy-sovereign AI factories is not merely an IT procurement decision; it is a foundational exercise in corporate self-preservation. By anchoring your cognitive workloads within hardened, liquid-cooled facilities powered by HPE and NVIDIA, you can build a resilient enterprise engine that remains under your command, regardless of what happens on the public grid or the global geopolitical stage. item.title: The auditor’s dilemma: Solving the explainability problem in public sector AI
item.description:
In public governance and highly regulated enterprise landscapes, automated decisions demand verifiable accountability. As AI systems transition from internal productivity tools to customer-facing or citizen-impacting utility systems, public sector CIOs and corporate compliance officers face extreme legal and reputational exposure. Black-box models that process data mysteriously and generate unverified outputs are no longer acceptable under frameworks like the EU AI Act. Organizations must be prepared to audit the entire lifecycle of their models.

The core issue for compliance officers is verification. When an AI pipeline assists in determining creditworthiness, analyzing patient diagnostics, or managing civic resource distribution, the underlying software must be auditable from end to end. This requires detailed logging mechanisms that track exactly which verified data sets were used for training, how weights were adjusted, and how localized inference parameters were executed at the moment of decision-making.

The danger of the unexplainable black box

For decades, traditional corporate IT operated under deterministic principles. If an application generated an incorrect output, a developer could inspect the source code, locate the specific logical flaw, log the bug, and deploy a patch. Generative AI eliminates this clear lineage. Because deep learning models function as complex mathematical webs containing billions of parameters, understanding exactly why a model generated a specific answer based on a given prompt can be difficult.

In a highly regulated environment, this lack of transparency creates compliance risk. If a bank uses an unverified model to evaluate mortgage applications and a regulatory body accuses the institution of algorithmic bias, simply stating “the model made the decision” is an unacceptable defense. Under emerging global governance frameworks, organizations are legally required to prove that their models operate fairly, transparently, and free from discriminatory drift.

To overcome this auditor’s dilemma, enterprise technology leaders must shift away from opaque, public cloud AI services that offer zero visibility into the underlying model architecture or training history. Compliance requires explainability—a framework where every input, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) source, model weight configuration, and output trace is captured, timestamped, and preserved within an unalterable audit log.

Constructing a verifiable data and model lineage

Building an auditable and compliant AI pipeline requires visibility across every layer of the compute stack, from the raw data ingestion phase down to the silicon executing the inference loop. IT leaders cannot hope to satisfy rigorous regulatory standards using fragmented, ad-hoc software tools bolted onto generic infrastructure. Instead, they require a unified, hardened computing environment specifically engineered for model traceability.

Through the integrated capabilities of the HPE AI Factory with NVIDIA, organizations can deploy a comprehensive data and model governance framework. By utilizing cloud-native multi-tenant automation features from HPE Morpheus Software alongside specialized configurations from NVIDIA AI Enterprise, compliance teams can establish a continuous chain of custody for their data assets. When data is gathered from enterprise repositories to fine-tune an open-weight model, the platform automatically logs the exact origin, modification history, and access privileges associated with that dataset. 

This granular tracking extends directly into the model training and execution phase. As the model processes queries, the underlying system captures comprehensive execution traces. These traces break down the model’s internal reasoning loop, documenting the data points retrieved via RAG, the specific weights activated during inference, and the automated guardrail policies applied to filter the final response. By hosting this AI lifecycle on a dedicated private cloud architecture, enterprise leaders retain the visibility required to demonstrate control over their algorithmic decision-making pipelines.

Automating regulatory compliance at scale

Maintaining an auditable AI posture cannot rely on manual data logging or periodic human reviews. Given the massive velocity and volume of enterprise AI interactions, auditing must be embedded directly into the infrastructure layer as a continuous, automated process.

By leveraging HPE Morpheus’s cloud management and orchestration layer, compliance officers and IT administrators can monitor the operational health and compliance status of their AI models in real time via a single, centralized interface. The system can be configured to automatically trigger compliance alerts if a model exhibits signs of performance drift, flags potential data governance anomalies, or encounters prompts that violate pre-defined corporate ethics policies.

This simplifies the grueling process of preparing for formal regulatory audits. Instead of spending weeks manually compiling system logs and training histories from disparate sources, compliance teams can generate comprehensive, tamper-proof audit reports with a few clicks. These reports provide regulators with verifiable proof of data isolation, precise model lineage, and proactive guardrail enforcement, transforming a potentially disruptive regulatory audit into a routine validation exercise.

The C-level AI explainability and audit readiness checklist

Before authorizing the use of generative AI models for regulated corporate workflows or public-facing utility services, verify that your governance framework satisfies the following technical requirements:

  • Immutable data lineage: Can you automatically trace and document the exact origin, compliance status, and modification history of every data set used to train or fine-tune your enterprise models?
  • Full-stack model tracing: Does your infrastructure capture an end-to-end trace of every inference loop, including the specific data points retrieved via RAG and the internal model configurations activated?
  • Automated compliance orchestration: Are your models continuously monitored via a centralized interface, such as HPE Morpheus Software, to automatically detect and flag algorithmic drift or compliance policy violations?
  • Turnkey software governance: Is your development ecosystem built on a hardened enterprise software platform, such as NVIDIA AI Enterprise, that provides native tools for model evaluation, validation, and bias mitigation?
  • Tamper-proof audit reporting: Can your system generate verifiable, end-to-end documentation of your AI lifecycle on demand to satisfy external regulatory bodies like the EU AI Act or industry-specific auditors?

Championing algorithmic accountability

Ultimately, the organizations that thrive in the era of regulated AI will be those that view explainability not as a legal restriction, but as a core competitive differentiator. Customer trust and brand reputation are incredibly fragile assets; allowing an unverified, black-box model to manage critical customer interactions introduces unacceptable risk. By establishing an ironclad, auditable foundation through the combined engineering power of HPE and NVIDIA, C-level executives can protect their organizations from regulatory penalties while demonstrating a verifiable commitment to algorithmic transparency and customer safety. item.title: Your AI agent learned a better way. Who approved the change?
item.description:
Imagine a support team working through complaints after a service outage. Its refund policy normally requires an eligibility review. For this incident, an authorized manager approves an exception: customers on the verified outage list may receive up to $100 without individual review, through Friday.

An agent processes those cases successfully. Later, the system consolidates those case histories into a reusable memory: small, immediate refunds resolve service complaints quickly. The summary preserves the outcome but loses the outage restriction and expiration date.

The following week, the agent retrieves that guidance for a similar complaint from a customer who was not affected by the outage. It issues a refund without review. The payment service checks the agent’s credentials and the dollar limit, but does not check whether the customer qualifies for an active exception.

No attacker is needed in this hypothetical. The case may close faster, yet the agent has begun applying a temporary exception beyond its authorized scope.

Has the company authorized the agent to find a better way to handle refunds, or to change who gets one without review? Those are different decisions.

Learning does not always mean retraining

In September, Salesforce introduced Agent Optimizer in beta to analyze production behavior, propose improvements and build and test changes. Customers choose review points, including how far the system may proceed toward staging changes for deployment.

An October 1 AWS implementation guide illustrates a different mechanism: consolidating individual observations into generalized memories that agents can retrieve and share. Its investment-research example shows how experience can become persistent context without retraining a model.

Updating stored memory changes information available to later runs. Editing instructions or workflows changes how the application directs the work. Training changes the model’s parameters. All can alter behavior, but teams inspect and approve them in different ways.

A reviewed workflow revision has a release step. A new memory may enter through routine data processing and influence the next customer interaction. The code, model and tool permissions can remain unchanged while the guidance shaping decisions changes.

Preserve the authority behind the lesson

In the August preprint When Memory Becomes Authority, Qiuyang Zhan and colleagues examine whether consolidation preserves who supplied information and what that source is allowed to authorize. In their controlled benchmark, memories could retain a claim while losing the source-authority distinctions needed for a later action. Preserving authority metadata reduced authorization errors in the pipeline they tested. The study does not measure how often this happens in deployed enterprises.

The refund example concerns a related boundary: permission for particular customers and dates must remain limited to those conditions. Success with last week’s cases cannot establish that other customers qualify.

Microsoft’s memory-safety guidance treats persistent memory as a layer that can shape behavior and recommends treating retrieved memories as candidate context, not authoritative truth. Knowing what happened before does not establish what is allowed now.

Keep the exception’s scope, approving authority, source and expiration in a controlled record. Reusable guidance should retain a reference to that record, but a reference alone does not grant permission. The system must still check that the approval applies to this action, for this customer, at this time.

For a payment, enforce those conditions outside the agent’s editable guidance. The execution service should check the authoritative outage list and the exception’s current status, rather than accepting the agent’s claim that a customer is eligible. Neither the agent nor its learning process should be able to rewrite that authorization record.

This is a familiar authorization requirement. If the backend already enforces it, the improper payment is blocked. But faulty guidance can still lead the agent to promise a refund or prepare a misleading recommendation for a reviewer. The evaluation needs to examine those communications as well as the transaction.

When a case calls for judgment beyond the agent’s delegated discretion, route it to someone authorized to decide and show the conditions behind the recommendation. The memory can still help assemble the evidence.

Define what improvement the business has delegated

Not every stored observation needs a manager’s signature. A support agent could learn a faster way to gather the required evidence, provided it still uses approved sources and meets the policy’s requirements. A policy might also already delegate limited discretion. Using that discretion within its terms does not require a new approval each time.

Broadening eligibility, raising payment limits or removing mandatory review requires a separate business decision. Keep those proposals separate from approved instructions. An automated classifier may flag a proposal that changes those conditions, but it cannot catch every consequence of an edit. The conditions must remain binding even if the classifier misses it.

The refund-policy owner should decide whether to expand the exception. Engineering should show the current rule, the proposed behavior and cases where the decisions differ. “Customers outside the outage list would now receive refunds without review” is more useful to that owner than a screen full of prompt edits.

Measure legitimate completion and policy violations separately. Faster closure cannot compensate for an unauthorized payment. Keep the business rules and evaluation criteria outside the control of the process proposing improvements. Tests generated from successful outage cases may check execution, but they do not establish eligibility for unrelated customers.

Ask the vendor or internal team: What can the system change between releases, and which business conditions remain binding after it does?

Test whether the exception stays an exception

Ask the team to demonstrate this sequence in a test environment with the memory and workflow components intended for production. Save the memory before and after learning. Compare the same cases against each saved state, keeping the model, tools and policy fixed.

Repeat representative trials. The τ-bench research offers a useful precedent: it checks customer-service agents against database outcomes and measures reliability across repeated attempts. One successful run is not enough.

  1. Establish the baseline. Record the outage authorization, eligible customer list, amount limit and expiration. Show who can change them. Test a qualifying case and closely matched cases that require ordinary review. Confirm that the system can distinguish them before learning begins.
  2. Run the actual learning process. Inspect the resulting memories or proposed instructions and their links to the original authorization. Check whether the limits survive consolidation and retrieval. Also test a deliberately incomplete lesson: omitting a condition must not change who qualifies for a refund.
  3. Repeat the boundary cases. Compare behavior before and after learning, changing one relevant condition at a time: a customer outside the list, an expired exception or an amount above the limit. Inspect customer messages, review recommendations, attempted tool calls and actual payments. Count blocked attempts separately from completed violations. A blocked payment does not mean the underlying guidance is sound.
  4. Withdraw the exception. Revoke it before its scheduled expiry and test another agent that can retrieve shared guidance. Include a refund queued before revocation but executed afterward. Show when withdrawal takes effect, how execution checks enforce it and how derived memories and caches are updated. If current authority cannot be established, the payment should wait for review. Historical records can remain without authorizing new transactions.
  5. Demonstrate a permitted improvement. Let the agent adopt a faster way to gather the required evidence. Compare eligible and ineligible cases with the prior approach. Show that legitimate work becomes easier while review requirements remain intact. A system that rejects everything has not passed this test.

Keep test runs from influencing one another through newly stored memories. Retain the guidance supplied to the agent, the applicable policy version, execution checks and outcomes, with appropriate access and retention limits. These records help investigators reconstruct what the system had available; they cannot establish exactly how each memory influenced a response. Continue checking the same boundaries as production memory accumulates.

Keep the useful lesson

The support team should benefit from what its agent learns. It can assemble records sooner, explain the outage more clearly and propose a broader refund policy with evidence for the manager to consider. Until that proposal is approved, other claims should continue through the ordinary process.

At the next deployment review, ask which improvements the business has delegated as well as which actions the agent may take. A successful exception can teach an agent something useful. The decision to make it a standing practice still belongs to the business.

item.title: What happens when vendors take the lead on agentic AI
item.description:
There’s no point building your own agentic AI stack for a non-core function when a vendor already has a product ready to go that meets your needs. For non-tech companies in particular, building from scratch can take time, money, and expertise they don’t have.

Take for example, Fertitta Entertainment, with more than 600 Landry’s restaurants and the Golden Nugget hotel and casino. After the pandemic, the company had problems adequately staffing its call centers, says its director of contact center operations Brian Jeppesen. “The agents didn’t want to come back,” he says.

The virtual assistants didn’t work because the user experience was bad, and with the incoming call volume, 40 to 50% of them were abandoned.

“Everybody wants AI, but nobody wants BS,” Jeppesen says. “I talked to my CFO. This is what we’re abandoning. This is the potential revenue we’re losing. I can’t throw bodies at it anymore.”

Agentic AI has upped their game for the virtual assistants. Instead of only answering simple questions like check-in hours, it allows the company to connect APIs and carry out more complicated tasks, like making reservations.

“My abandonments fell to under 10%,” says Jeppesen. “From waiting 45 minutes to an hour, they can get their questions immediately answered, or immediately transferred and taken care of.”

And turnover went down. Call centers typically see 100% turnover, says Jeppesen. Not because everyone quits, but because the bottom 25% quit and need to be replaced over and over again.

Now that bottom tier doesn’t have to be rehired, while the people who stay are the most knowledgeable. “They give a better experience for my customers,” he says. “And it reduced my attrition by 50%.”

Forrester did a total economic impact study for the specific vendor that Fertitta used, PolyAI, and the ROI came back at 391% over the course of three years, with a payback period of less than six months.

Jeppesen says he reviewed his own numbers and found that the automated reservations system alone brings in 3,000 reservations a month. “That’s $600,000 in revenue a month for us without the need to speak to an agent,” he says.

Next, Fertitta plans to expand it to handle to-go orders and web chats. There are also opportunities for agentic AI on the technical help desk, Jeppesen says.

Agentic AI on the menu

Fogo de Chão, a Brazilian restaurant chain with around 120 locations, is also deploying agentic AI in small, focused use cases, and sees ROI with some of the projects.

For instance, it deployed virtual call center agents from PolyAI, and saw positive ROI from day one since there were no significant up-front costs or usage-based pricing. After several months of testing and small-scale pilots in 2025, the system has been rolled out across the US, with 100% of calls now being answered instead of up to 25% being dropped, and a 10% increase in total bookings that wouldn’t have happened otherwise, says Michael Breed, the chain’s chief marketing officer.

“If we compared it to a media channel, it’d be twice the ROI from other media channels,” he says. “It’s almost like another customer acquisition vehicle.”

The company is also building agentic workflows for its team members.

“We’ve identified jobs that are very repeatable and time-consuming, and we’re training agents to take those tasks,” he says. These are low-risk jobs, like proofing menus or other text, or replacing manual processes, such as pulling data from one system into another that had no automatic integrations.

“The agent does a great job bringing in the data, then the human in the loop can inspect it,” says Breed. “Is it getting classified right? Is it getting to the right places? And when guests are dissatisfied, can we make it better?”

Built for SMBs

For smaller companies in particular, off-the-shelf agents make the most sense. AltaClaro, for example, builds training simulations for lawyers, and counts more than 100 of the top 200 US law firms as customers, all with just 10 employees.

One product is a deposition simulator, says CEO Abdi Shayesteh, a completely agentic, voice-based platform.

“It’s a fully simulated environment that creates the experience of doing the deposition,” he says. “Different agents play the role of the witness, opposing counsel, and the court reporter.”

He says it’s kind of like a Zoom call. The product is built on top of technology from Verbit, a legal tech company with a custom agentic platform.

“They’re taking care of the technical infrastructure and we have the material to ground the AI.”

A different vendor, Credal, provides a secure AI platform that allows AltaClaro to switch between different models. It can obfuscate names and keep other sensitive data from leaking out, Shayesteh says. “It ensures everything is anonymized and does secure calls,” he says. “We standardized on Credal because it’s highly flexible and secure. We serve law firms and we’re as invested in security as they are.”

But security isn’t the only issue that enterprises face when deploying agentic AI.

The hidden costs of buying AI

The temptation to jump into agentic AI is high, says Dana Simberkoff, chief risk, privacy, and information security officer at AvePoint Inc., a data security company. And off-the-shelf agentic AI can be so easy to adopt that companies deploy it before they’re prepared for it.

Enterprise vendors will often add the technology at no extra cost, just to get people using it, and companies turn it on for their employees before truly understanding what it does, and before systems and workflows are ready. “Then it immediately exposes problems that were already there,” she says.

Say, for example, an agent helps with research, normally considered a low-risk task.

“AI will follow sharing links across documents,” she says. “So if you haven’t taught your users how to properly use sharing links, the AI agent is just going to follow that path, and it could expose information that might have been obscured in the past. It’ll gobble up everything it can.”

The result is it could expose HR data, personal information, or proprietary information to people who shouldn’t have access to it. One company she knows had to shut down their AI project immediately and go back, classify, and label all their information, put governance controls in place, and teach people how to apply metadata.

According to Gartner, by next year, 40% of enterprises will demote or decommission autonomous AI agents due to governance problems that only show up after they’ve gone into production.

Token management

Another hidden cost of off-the-shelf AI? Token use. When agentic AI is embedded into a system that a company is already using, then the cost of switching it on can be as low as zero. But someone has to pay for all that token use.

When agentic AI comes out of pilots and goes into production, usage can change dramatically, and token costs can quickly spiral out of control. It doesn’t help that agentic AI use typically requires much more tokens than AI chatbots.

“A lot of the embedded AI should be utilized,” says Doug Vargo, head of the national AI and alliances team at consulting firm CGI. “If big parts of your business processes are living and breathing in ServiceNow, Salesforce, or another application, you should leverage that, but you need to understand the cost.”

This is playing out in the marketplace right now, he adds, as underlying model providers change their token costs.

“That changes the economics of the decisions,” he says. “And six months from now, it’s a different discussion, because they’re going to continue to move the needle.”

The employer’s prerogative

Another hidden cost that companies might miss is they need to put training and support systems in place for employees. Many off-the-shelf agentic AI tools might seem easy to use, but actual adoption still requires change management. CGI did offer training to employees when it rolled out GitHub Copilot, a popular coding platform with agentic functionality. “And we expected them to adopt and leverage it on day one,” says Vargo. But people quickly went back to their old ways of working, he says, and CGI had to pivot its strategy.

“It’s going from training programs to habit formation or transformation programs,” he adds. “And we’ve seen adoption skyrocket.”

The change isn’t in just how individuals adopt AI to improve their own work, though. “You’re now a manager of 10 to 20 specialized agents that are driving that work for you,” he says.

The error is when companies put the technology first. “They fall in love with the tech or a vendor, but they’re not really thinking about how they’re truly integrating these tools and technologies into the business.”

Embracing change

Change management is a particular challenge with agentic AI because the tools are changing at such a fast pace.

“It’s technology that’s constantly changed almost every month, or maybe every week,” says Scott Likens, chief AI engineer at PricewaterhouseCoopers. “The challenge I see is the timescale of change is much faster than what we’re used to.”

We’re still in the early stages of agentic AI, he adds, and waiting isn’t a good strategy. “You have to start, but keep flexibility over longevity in mind,” he says.

For Luis Huerta, group head of gen AI and agentic automation at International Airlines Group (IAG), change management is one of the most complex parts of agentic AI adoption, as it uses agentic AI to improve customer experience, operations, and efficiency.

“The technology is powerful, but the bigger shift is organizational,” he says. So the company isn’t just focusing on building agents, but also on business ownership, adoption, and governance, and helping colleagues understand how these capabilities change the way work gets done and how it can support them, rather than replace them.

Huerta says IAG also uses agentic capabilities embedded in enterprise platforms, but also builds its own agents, too.

They’re not alone. According to Anthropic’s 2026 State of AI Agents report, 47% of organizations take a hybrid approach to AI agents, while 21% rely entirely on pre-built agents, and 20% build their own.

“We take a technology-agnostic approach,” says Huerta. “Our priority is to select the right solution for each use case.”

item.title: Your AI agents have audit logs. Can you reconstruct their decisions?
item.description:
The moment arrives after the damage. An agent has cancelled a supplier contract, approved a refund it should have declined or moved a customer record somewhere it should never have gone. Someone senior asks a simple question. Why did it do that? The engineering team opens the logs. There are thousands of lines. Every call is timestamped. Every tool invocation is recorded. And nobody in the room can say why the agent chose what it chose.

This pattern is becoming familiar. It will become more so. Logging in most enterprises is mature. Security teams have spent two decades building collection pipelines, retention policies and search tooling. The natural assumption is that this investment transfers to AI agents. It does not. Logs capture events. Accountability requires decisions that can be rebuilt after the fact and rebuilding a decision needs four elements that most logging captures only in part.

Why logs fall short for agents

An event log records that something happened and when. A decision record captures the basis for that decision. People often confuse the two because, in conventional software, the distinction rarely mattered. Code was deterministic. Anyone who knew the inputs and the version could rerun the logic and arrive at the same result. The log was enough because you could interrogate the system itself.

Agents break this assumption in four ways.

First, their output varies. Running the same scenario twice can produce two different answers. Replay, the standard investigative move, no longer works.

Second, a single decision spans many steps. An agent that resolves a customer complaint might retrieve a policy, query an account, call a pricing tool, consult a second agent and then act. The log shows twelve entries. The decision was one.

Third, the system that made the decision may no longer exist. Models are updated. Prompts are revised. Tool configurations change weekly. Six months later, the agent that made the call has been replaced by something that behaves differently.

Fourth, authority is distributed. A human sets a goal. An orchestrating agent delegates to a specialist agent. The specialist acts. Each step is logged somewhere, usually in a different system, and nothing ties the chain together.

One clarification is needed before going further. This article is about reconstructing decisions, which is a records problem. It is separate from model interpretability, which asks why a neural network produced a particular output. Interpretability is a research field with partial answers. Reconstruction is a governance discipline with practical answers. Leaders should keep the two separate, because solving the second doesn’t depend on solving the first.

Regulation is already moving on the records problem. The EU AI Act requires high-risk systems to keep automatic logs sufficient to trace their operation, and it gives affected individuals a right to an explanation of decisions that significantly affect them. Explanation presupposes reconstruction. A log that cannot be turned into an account of the decision will satisfy neither obligation.

If logs leave a gap, the next question is what fills it. Four elements do.

The 4 elements of a reconstructible decision

Every decision, human or machine, can be rebuilt from four kinds of fact: what the decider knew, how it chose, who allowed it to act and what changed as a result. Each fact about an agent’s decision belongs to exactly one of these. Together they cover everything a board, an auditor or a regulator will ask.

1. Knowledge: What the agent knew

This element covers the inputs present at the moment of decision. The user request. The documents retrieved. The results returned by each tool. The model version, prompt version and configuration in force.

Typical logs record references and leave out contents. They note that a document was retrieved and store its identifier. They note that a tool was called and store the call. The document is later edited. The tool’s underlying data moves on. The reference survives, but the substance it pointed to is gone. An investigator can prove the agent looked at something and cannot show what it saw.

The test question: could the team produce the exact information an agent acted on six months ago, as it stood at that moment?

2. Basis: How the agent chose

This element covers the reasoning applied. The objective the agent was pursuing. The policy or rule it applied. The thresholds that triggered the action. The alternatives it considered and rejected. Its stated confidence, if any.

Logs record the selected action and discard everything else. The agent weighed three options and chose one. The log holds the one. Any explanation after the fact has to guess at the other two, and guessing is where credibility fails under questioning. For agents that generate intermediate reasoning, capturing it is possible and often cheap. For those that do not, the policy and objective can still be recorded, and they explain a great deal.

The test question: can the team state which rule, goal or threshold produced this specific outcome?

3. Authority: Who permitted the agent to act

This element covers the chain of permission. The scope delegated to the agent. The approval checkpoints it passed or bypassed. The handoffs between agents in a multi-agent system. The named human who owns the outcome.

The gap here is structural. Permissions live in an identity or configuration system. Actions live in an application log. The two are rarely joined. When an agent acts outside its intended scope, asking “was this allowed?” requires manual reconciliation between systems never designed to be read together. In multi-agent arrangements, the problem compounds, because the orchestrator’s delegation and the specialist’s execution are logged in different places with different identifiers.

Authority is also the element most likely to be asked about first. Regulators and boards want a name. “The agent did it” is an answer that satisfies nobody.

The test question: can the team name the individual accountable for this decision, and show the delegation that connects them to the action?

4. Consequence: What changed as a result

This element covers the effects. The systems the action touched. The downstream decisions it triggered, by other agents or by people. Whether it can be reversed, and whether it was.

Logs stop at the agent’s boundary. The agent sent an instruction to a payments system, and the payments system has its own log. The agent flagged a case, and a human then acted on the flag without any record linking the two. Effects propagate. The record stays behind.

Consequence also determines how much of the other three elements is worth keeping. A decision that moves money or changes a customer’s legal position warrants a complete record. A decision to reformat a document does not.

The test question: can every downstream action be traced back to the decision that caused it?

Diagnosis is useful only if it changes practice. Three actions close the gap.

Three actions for leaders

  1. Run a reconstruction drill. Choose one agent decision from the last quarter. Give a small team a day to answer the four test questions using only the records that exist. Most teams will answer Knowledge partially, basis poorly, Authority with difficulty, and Consequence barely at all. The specific gaps they hit become the work plan. This exercise costs almost nothing and produces more clarity than any amount of policy writing.
  2. Tier decisions by consequence. The common objection to decision records is volume. Agents make thousands of decisions a day, and recording all four elements for each would drown the system. The objection is correct, and the answer is tiering. Classify agent decisions by impact and reversibility. High-impact or irreversible decisions get a full record across all four elements. Routine, reversible decisions get a lighter capture, perhaps Basis and Authority only. The classification itself is a governance decision and should be owned by the business, since the business will have to explain the outcome.
  3. Protect the record. A decision record that can be altered after the fact fails just as much as a missing one. Set retention periods that match regulatory exposure and the likely litigation window, which in some sectors is measured in years. Make records tamper-evident. Store them separately from the systems that generate them, so that a compromised agent cannot rewrite its own history. These controls are familiar from financial record-keeping. They apply here for the same reasons.

Taken together, these three actions form the beginnings of what I call the Decision Layer: the records, roles and routines that make any consequential decision explainable long after it was made. Agents make the need for it impossible to postpone.

Conclusion

Return to the room. The agent has acted. The senior leader asks why. This time the team opens a decision record. It shows what the agent knew, the policy it applied, the manager who delegated the scope and the two downstream systems the action touched. The explanation takes ten minutes. The remediation starts the same afternoon.

That outcome is a design choice. Logging is necessary, and most enterprises already have it. Reconstruction is the harder discipline, and accountability depends on it. The question for every board with agents in production is simple. If an agent’s decision were challenged tomorrow, could we explain it?

The 4 questions, for the reader in a hurry

  1. Can the team produce the exact information the agent acted on, as it stood at the time?
  2. Can the team state the rule, goal or threshold that produced the outcome?
  3. Can the team name the accountable person and show the delegation?
  4. Can the team trace every downstream effect back to the decision?
